summary: This Wikipedia article covers lithium, the chemical element with symbol Li and atomic number 3. It describes lithium as a soft, silvery-white alkali metal that is the least dense metal and solid element, highly reactive, and never found free in nature. The note also covers its physical properties, isotopes, nuclear significance, cosmic and terrestrial occurrence, and industrial and medical uses.
one_line: Overview of lithium, the lightest alkali metal and element 3, covering its physical properties, isotopes, cosmic and terrestrial occurrence, and uses.
key_facts: Lithium has symbol Li and atomic number 3, and is a soft, silvery-white alkali metal.
Under standard conditions, lithium is the least dense metal and the least dense solid element.
Lithium must be stored in vacuum, inert atmosphere, or inert liquid such as purified kerosene or mineral oil because it is highly reactive and flammable.
Lithium metal is isolated electrolytically from a mixture of lithium chloride and potassium chloride.
The transmutation of lithium atoms to helium in 1932 was the first fully human-made nuclear reaction.

Lithium and its compounds are used in heat-resistant glass and ceramics, lithium grease lubricants, flux additives, lithium metal batteries, and lithium-ion batteries, which consume more than three-quarters of lithium production.
Lithium's melting point is 180.50 °C (453.65 K) and its boiling point is 1,342 °C (1,615 K) according to the infobox's standard values.
Lithium has a density of 0.534 g/cm3, comparable with pine wood, and is one of only three metals that can float on water.
Naturally occurring lithium consists of two stable isotopes, lithium-6 and lithium-7, with lithium-7 at 95.15% natural abundance.
Lithium is less common in the Solar System than 25 of the first 32 chemical elements.
Lithium was discovered by Johan August Arfwedson in 1817 and first isolated by William Thomas Brande in 1821.
Seawater contains lithium at about 0.14 to 0.25 ppm, and the total lithium content of seawater is estimated at 230 billion tonnes.
Estimates for Earth's crustal lithium content range from 20 to 70 ppm by weight.
Lithium-based drugs are useful as a mood stabilizer and antidepressant in treating mental illness such as bipolar disorder.
On 27 May 2020, astronomers reported that classical nova explosions are galactic producers of lithium-7.
